content: Endometriosis is a prevalent gynecological condition that can cause significant pain and infertility in women. It has a profound impact on their quality of life, affecting their professional lives, daily activities, and both sexual and nonsexual relationships, as well as their fertility. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are commonly used as the first-line treatment for managing pain associated with endometriosis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of NSAIDs in managing pain in women with endometriosis, comparing them to placebo, other NSAIDs, alternative pain management drugs, or no treatment at all. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, and trial registries, up to October 2016. However, no new randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified for inclusion in this update. The review included two trials overall, but only one trial involving 24 women was analyzed. The methodological details of the included trial were insufficient, leading to an unclear risk of bias. The quality of the evidence was assessed as very low using the GRADE approach, primarily due to the small sample size, wide confidence intervals, and risk of bias. The comparison of NSAIDs (specifically naproxen) versus placebo did not demonstrate any significant benefit in pain relief for women with endometriosis. The odds ratio (OR) for pain relief was 3.27, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.61 to 17.69, based on one trial with 24 participants. The evidence was of very low quality. Similarly, there was no conclusive evidence to suggest that women taking NSAIDs (naproxen) were less likely to require additional analgesia (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.29) or to experience side effects (OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.09 to 2.47) compared to those taking a placebo. These findings were also based on very low-quality evidence from the same single trial. The included studies did not provide any data on other important outcomes, such as quality of life, effects on daily activities, absence from work or school, the need for more invasive treatments, or participant satisfaction with the treatment. In conclusion, due to the lack of high-quality evidence and the absence of data on key outcomes, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the effectiveness of NSAIDs (naproxen) in managing pain associated with endometriosis. There is no evidence to suggest that one NSAID is more effective than another. As highlighted in other Cochrane reviews, women using NSAIDs should be aware of the potential for adverse effects associated with these medications.
